<reason>A high-quality, close debate. A built the cleaner path to the motion: the honor-vs-record framework was sustained from opening to closing, the "primarily" line was given a concrete historical test (defining act plus dedication record from Jim Crow/massive-resistance eras), and A's pressure questions forced B's two key concessions — a dictator's name can be stripped without defeat, and the Washington/Confederate difference is real — which A's closing credibly converted into "the line exists and B drew it." B fought back well: the orientation-vs-worship distinction and the act/inheritance philosophy were coherent answers to A's "reconferral" claim, and B's Q2 fork (mandate vs. preference) was its best moment, exposing real sloppiness in A4.4 ("the motion has done its work"). But A's closing repaired the fork for the cases B actually pressed (founders survive "primarily," so keeping them applies rather than evades the motion), while B never explained why inherited Jim Crow-era honorifics deserve permanent protection under its own criteria — its "rupture-only" position left it haggling over threshold with no standard of its own. B's slope argument also weakened once it conceded the historical difference is real. Both sides were disciplined: no fake citations, plausible examples throughout.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Rebuttal 1 was the most damaging single speech: it exposed B's double valuation of names (priceless when removed, weightless when kept) and deployed the new-school hypothetical — no one would name a school for a slaveholder today with a disclaimer attached, proving naming is honoring. B answered it philosophically (dedication ≠ inheritance), but the pressure shaped the rest of the debate. B's Rebuttal 2 fork ("if keeping Jefferson High satisfies the motion, the proposition fails as written; if not, 'case by case' was a mandate") was the strongest counter-thrust, but A neutralized it in the closing by tying compliance to the "primarily" standard rather than to process.</best_rebuttal>
